speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its deliberate and persistent undermining of the Parliamentary process, for its flouting of Parliamentary traditions and for its continuing attempts to reduce Parliament and Parliamentary government to an irrelevant appendix in the formulation and application of major national policy decisions and the expenditure of public funds, and demands that the Government immediately reverse its attitude of regarding Parliament as the private preserve of the Liberal Party thus hastening the restoration of respect for and the dignity of this institution.
He said: For a long time, Sir, we have been hearing about the erosion of Parliament. We have been hearing it from the Auditor General, hearing it from the media, from committees of this House, from the Opposition, and occasionally from a courageous backbencher on the Government side. It does not appear as though any of the warnings, admonitions or demands have had any effect whatsoever.
In spite of sweeping rules changes in 1968, it is clear that Parliament has never suffered so much by the neglect and abuse of Government as this Parliament at the present time. The rules changes have had the effect of weakening Parliament's control of the expenditure of public funds by removing the study of the estimates by the Committee of the Whole of this House. Certainly when the amount of business Parliament must contend with is considered, some measure was needed to relieve the pressures of those burdens on this House. But unfortunately, the net effect of all of the measures taken has been to weaken Parliament's control over the fiscal operations of this country.
One of the major problems is that Government has been operated by people who in their hearts really do not believe that Parliament is necessary. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made it clear in numerous statements that Parliament is an extraneous irrelevancy to the business of Government. The Prime Minister considers Parliament a nuisance. Indeed, in his some 15 years in office I dare say that he has not participated in debates in this House more than half a dozen times. Even more clearly has this appeared in the contempt with which he and his Government consistently address this House.
Let us just look at a few events in recent months. The Prime Minister unveils the Government's policy on the Cruise missile
in a letter to the press, with an accompanying note to suggest that in the interests of public information this had better be published. So we are now at a point where, from the august precincts of the Prime Minister's office, diktats are handed down for publication in the media for the enlightenment of a docile public. No tin pot dictator of a banana republic could have handled it more in accordance with the traditions of such institutions. Parliament has never been made aware in detail of the Government's policy position on the Cruise. We have not been given an opportunity to have the facts in this House. We have not been granted permission, even though we requested it on more than one occasion, to have before us the weapons testing agreement signed with the United States. This has never been ratified or debated by the elected representatives of the people in this House, yet this is a matter about which hundreds of thousands of Canadians have shown a well founded concern.
Canadians are concerned about the tergiversations, for want of a better term, of the Prime Minister in international policy, a policy which the House has not had the opportunity to debate. Instead of coming into the House and explaining the role and posture of Canada as an evenhanded broker between the United States and the Soviet Union, he elucidates his position in a long and detailed interview with a friendly Toronto newspaper. When he is pinned down on his criticisms, implied and direct, of the President of the United States, he attempts, unsuccessfully as it turns out, to backwater.
The point is that the debate is not carried in the House, where procedure, tradition and the highest demands of parliamentary freedom would suggest that it be carried on, but, rather, in the press, where the Prime Minister cannot be questioned, cannot be replied to, and his views cannot be tested.
What is the position of Parliament when the Prime Minister, acting strictly on his own, for purely political reasons, casts the nation in the dubious role of umpire or arbitrator between superpowers locked in nuclear confrontation? The concept of an evenhanded approach to the United States and the Soviet Union has never been debated or approved in the House. What does it mean? Are we to equate the actions of the aggressor with those of our friend and neighbour, our ally in NATO? Are we to erase all distinctions between the super slave power, whose aggressivity has cast a pall over Europe, Asia and Africa for 35 years, and the actions of the United States, whose foreign policy is aimed at preserving world peace and

stability? The Prime Minister obviously finds such distinctions to be oversimplistic, yet they are the distinctions which reside in the hearts and minds of Canadians who will resent being placed in a position of putting the United States and the U.S.S.R. on the same footing in Canadian foreign policy. None of this has ever come before the House for debate and resolution. Time and again, Parliament has been bypassed by the Government, frustrated by the continuing absence of Ministers and the continuing evasions on the Government benches.
There was a time when there were a few Ministers opposite who were honest and forthright in their answers to questions, but they are now all part of the same slippery bunch. We have had legislation dumped on us, literally dumped on us, poorly conceived and badly put together and, at the very best, ill-timed.
A year ago, for the first time in the House, the bells rang out for two weeks, an explosion of frustration and bitterness at the cavalier treatment of Parliament. At that time we were faced by a demand from the Government to rubberstamp an energy Bill containing elements of no less than 12 pieces of legislation, a demonstration of contempt for Parliament unequalled in many, many years.
We have had budgets tossed casually into the House and revised before the ink was dry. We have had budgets brought into the House, the only purpose of which was to revise the egregious errors of previous budgets. We had a proposal for the Crow rate thrown together in obvious haste and then altered before we had a chance to come to grips with it, and now altered again.
These Bills are writ on water. Parliament is not the same kind of quick lunch joint where the menu is changed every half hour. This is the public business. We have had Opposition days altered on a moment's notice by a Government which does not give a damn. Never has the public business been so poorly organized, so inadequately presented, so incompetently put together as under this Government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What about December of '79?

What do they want Parliament to do? Lie down and roll over? That is what they would like.
Regardless of the Prime Minister's opinion of Parliamentarians, Parliament will not do that unless, of course, the Government adopts the attitude which was adopted in Ghana when that new democracy modelled after Westminster was formed. The Government did not like the opposition there so it abolished it and threw half of them in jail. That is not going to happen here.
The sheer length and complexity of the Government business is another element in this Government's continuing contempt for the institution, its traditions and clear and central position in preserving the freedom of Canadians. No
Government has ever before in our history been so interventionist. This Government's centralizing policies have imposed upon Parliament a nearly insupportable burden of legislative quackery and parliamentary fiddle-faddle that no Parliament should have to put up with.
Because of this Government's inertia and incurable propensity to cover its tracks, we have had to take time out to extract the painful and distressing story of the clandestine arrangement between a former Minister and his colleagues in the Gillespie affair. We have been seized with the regrettable and sorry affair of another former Liberal Minister now before the courts. We have had the issue of a chairman of a major Crown corporation under investigation. In each of these areas the Government has thrown a smokescreen around Parliament's right to know. The official cover-up has gone into play.
In spite of the whiff of corruption emanating from that side, we are put off with the excuse that the matter is under investigation. These exercises in insider corruption within the Liberal Party do not serve to enhance the image of the Liberal Party.
There are Members on that side who are just as scandalized and just as disillusioned as we are in these matters. There are honest Members on the Government side. They are decent, hardworking Parliamentarians with an abiding respect for the institution and its traditions who are shocked and put off most strongly at the way in which Parliament is being degraded under this Government. They are concerned, as we are, at the parallel Government which is the personal creation of the Prime Minister, a caricature of Government, run by his flunkies which the Prime Minister has instituted to carry out his personal ideology. It is referred to by the Auditor General as a Government within a Government. The spidery network of Crown corporations and agencies, holding companies and quasi private corporations operated from the Prime Minister's office constitute a threat to the freedom of this country. What he cannot do by the front door, he is trying to do by the back door.
Parliament stands in the way of the socialization of this nation against the popular will. Therefore he is attempting to bring it about extra-legally and extra-curricularly by using public funds and the efforts of men who are sworn to carry out the wishes of the Prime Minister. This man has more court favourites than Louis XIV and each one has his own private little kingdom to operate at the taxpayers' expense.
It is true that they go through the motions of bringing these matters to Parliament, but well after the fact. What will the House of Commons do with 1,400 gas stations? Perhaps they will serve as a place of employment for Grit flunkies after the next election.
Continuing contempt, disregard, neglect and abuse of Parliament has been the hallmark of this Government. From the buffoonery of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in front of the TV cameras with his budget papers to the backing and filling of the Prime Minister in delicate international matters of primary concern to Canadians, Parliament has been told to take a back seat.
June 6, 1983

It has been made clear to this House, elected to serve and to represent Canadians in the same way as the Prime Minister was elected, that we have all been red circled. This House has been kept sitting here longer than any Parliament in the history of this country, including the "long Parliament, of Charles I. We have not had a Throne Speech in nearly four years. What does that mean? It means there has been no blueprint of Government plans, no blueprint of Government intentions, so that Parliament has been kept deliberately in the dark. I would venture to suggest, Sir, that if Parliament is in the dark it is not more so than the Cabinet itself, whose members are usually the last to know about the Prime Minister's intentions.
Parliament has been inhibited in carrying out its functions. This House has been prevented from acting on major national issues, such as unemployment, high interest rates, bankruptcies and the sliding of the economy down the slippery slope of recession simply because this Government has removed its expenditures from the control of Parliament. As a result, Canadians everywhere have suffered. They have been subject to policies of economic attrition. They have been made to pay in lost jobs, lost income, higher taxes for the inefficiencies of an arrogant Government wrapped in a cloak of its own isolation. We are now in the clearly unconstitutional position of going into the fourth year of this Parliament without a new session, another indication of the Government's contempt for those traditions and laws which have made parliamentary democracy the envy of the world.
Only Parliament stands in the way of the Prime Minister's attempt to create a kind of corporatist state in this country. In order to do this, it is necessary for him to break or to bypass the power of the House of Commons, weakened though it may be. He has been working very hard at doing so-
Who wrote that nonsense?
-and the time has come to call a halt and bring this Government back to the realization that it is not going to be able to govern without the consent of Parliament.
Hear, hear!

This is the purpose of the motion before the House now, perhaps the most serious ever to come before the House of Commons since I have been here. This country cannot operate in freedom with Parliament shunted to the sidelines, as it has been under this Government.
1 described the motion before the House as extremely serious, and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) laughs. That is one further indication of the mental attitude that exists over there with regard to the Government's contempt of this institution.

That is arrogance.

Another Member, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) shows the same degree of contempt for this institution about which I am speaking. Liberal Members do not understand this place. That is very sad, Sir.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The Hon. Member for Yukon has the floor.

On the grounds of competence alone, Parliament cannot be a dumping ground of badly conceived legislation, half-baked budgetary attempts that must be constantly revised, and disorganized House business. Parliament is entitled to be treated with respect. This is a lesson which the Government and those who support it seem unable to learn. The Prime Minister must cease and desist his attempts to create a parallel Government to wrest control of the purse strings from the House of Commons and to relegate Parliament to a back seat in the decision-making process.
One of Parliament's primary functions is to prevent the excesses of Government. This Government has done everything possible to inhibit Parliament's role. The purpose of this motion is to attempt to bring home to the Government and to the Prime Minister that he must cease his performance as some kind of sun king, that he cannot expect to create important foreign policy in the media, particularly when it involves a role of which Parliament has never approved and threatens our relations with our allies. This Government and those who support it must be brought to realize that Parliament's role is not to be diminished or curtailed but rather the opposite.
Canada is not ready for a one-man government, even if the Liberal Party is. God help us if the country ever reaches the stage which the Prime Minister is attempting to bring about. Parliament is now at a crisis in its long history in the country. If the Government, which has attempted to control the media, the private sector and to downgrade the role of the Provinces, continues in its determination to govern without Parliament, then the Government has voted in favour of its own terminal decay.
I hope Hon. Members on the Government side will rise to participate in this debate and, in so doing, justify if they can and I challenge them to do so-the number of occasions since they came back in 1980 where they have bypassed and thwarted the parliamentary process deliberately by reason of the fact that they regarded it as some kind of private, personal perserve of the Liberal Party.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). He complained at the beginning of his speech that Parliament did not have an opportunity to discuss international affairs. He knows very well that under the rules this matter can be raised on an Opposition day, as is the case today. This subject could have been chosen and would have been much more appropriate and serious. Could the Hon. Member explain why this subject was not chosen for today, and where is his critic for international affairs?

I suppose the President of the Privy Council can be forgiven-and I say this with generosity and without offence-simply because he has not been here long enough to appreciate the standard annual practice which existed in this place prior to the election of the present Prime Minister, where external and foreign affairs were debated on an annual basis on days that were put up by the Government. Earlier when I first came here two days of Government time were allotted back to back for the purpose of debating external affairs. 1 must say that as a result of that kind of practice there was a far closer harmony, which there should be, between Opposition and Government benches on external and foreign affairs, because that is the manner in which we should appear on the international stage when it comes to that exceptional policy area.
When the Prime Minister was elected that changed. The President of the Privy Council indicated the practice when he first came into the House. He will also admit that it changed with the changes of rules. Now, because the Government-and I say "Government" because its majority passed these changes-allotted us a specific number of days, it expects us to use our days as it sees fit. They are our choice, not the Government's choice. It would like to determine the subject matter of those days, but that is one of the freedoms that still rests with us. I hope that adequately answers the question of the President of the Privy Council.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not at all, Mr. Speaker. Once again the Hon. Member for Yukon has led us to believe that the change in the rules which gave the Opposition 25 Opposition days per year was passed because of the Liberal majority. That is simply not true. That is not the case.
It was passed by closure.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was not even passed by closure. No, that is not the truth. What we are talking about here is what happened in December 1967 or 1969.
It was 1969.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It was before I was here, 1969. It was by unanimous consent of the House of Commons that those rules were adopted. I invite my hon. colleagues to check the record.
You had better do that.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The 25 Opposition days were supported by the entire House of Commons in 1969. When they talk about closure, they are talking about Standing Order 75A, 75B and
75C. That was not part of the package. He should know more about the business of supply which was supported unanimously by the House of Commons in 1969.
The Opposition now have 25 days a year in which to select a subject of their choice. They have dealt with other matters but it seems they were not interested in choosing international affairs. The Hon. Member said that it was up to the Government to use its time. Perhaps we could have afforded more time if the bells had not rung for 17 days during the last two years. Despite that, this morning could have been a very good day to be used by the Opposition to deal with international matters. That subject was there to be taken by the external affairs critic of the Tory Party.
The Hon. Member did not answer my questions. Why did they not choose that important subject this morning, and where is their critic on the subject?

To answer the question very, very quickly, I dealt with this subject in the light of the motion. I have dealt with the very subject which the President of the Privy Council is criticizing me for not dealing with. Let him not speak to us about 25 days. Let him not charge us with holding up the business of Parliament when that business was so abused by the process they attempted that our only recourse was to ring those bells. Let those opposite not talk to me about holding up the parliamentary process when they themselves in 1963 kept the government of the day of then Prime Minister Diefenbaker for 49 days-a record in the House of Commons-by filibustering tactics, forcing the government of the day to go to Governor General's warrants to get enough to pay the civil service. Let not the accusers over there talk to me about holding up the parliamentary process.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen). While my colleagues in the New Democratic Party and I join with him in much of his criticism of the arrogance of the Government and what we also regard as its contempt for Parliament and for public opinion, I must say that I found it passing strange to hear the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the Conservative Party in the House of Commons condemning the Government for its failure-a criticism which is justified-to bring before the House in a Government-sponsored debate or motion, for instance, the question of the agreement to test the Cruise missile in Canada. I found it particularly strange in view of the comments of the Conservative defence critic, the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), on April 29, 1982, when my Party gave up its allotted time to enable a defence and foreign policy debate. At that point the Hon. Member for Victoria said:
The second recommendation is that there be no Cruise missile testing in Canada. I have many reasons as to why we cannot and should not support such a recommendation. However, I will limit myself in this short and gratis time to saying that we-

Since his coming into this House, I have noticed that he is prone to twisting, distorting and changing colour in order to suit the public opinion of the day. That Hon. Member's opinion cannot be accepted on any matter. All he does is twist, ride and distort for the purpose of pushing the so-called socialist position on anything: always grandstanding, like the Member in front of him. He is always attempting to grab an issue and then be very annoyed when he cannot do so.
That is understandable because (a) they are Members of the New Democratic Party; therefore, that explains a lot; and (b), they are in deep trouble in this country so they grab at anything they think will lift them up by their bootstraps, if they can see a way of doing it. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would just point out to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) that he has a short and selective memory. During this session of Parliament, in the Summer of 1980, the Government did in fact allocate two days of Government time to a debate on international affairs. That, of course, was before we got into the constitutional filibustering and the bell ringing. If there has been any breach of parliamentary tradition, it has not been on this side of the House.
I realize my time is short, Mr. Speaker, so I will keep my answer short. That intervention amounted to a crock of rhubarb.

Mr. Speaker, I must confess that I found the answer of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) to my colleague's question almost tantamount to temporary insanity. I cannot believe that he would

attempt to worm his way out of the clear and unequivocal statement that is contained in the answer with regard to the Conservative position as it applies to the testing of nuclear weapons. It brings the debate down to a level I had hoped it would not reach.
I had intended, as you will appreciate, Mr. Speaker, to stay directly within the confines of the motion. I will, of course, do that, but I must draw to your attention in response to the comments by the Leader of the Opposition that any normal, reasonable individual reading page 16745 of the Commons Debates for April 29, 1982 would find the following words:
The second recommendation is that there be no Cruise missile testing in Canada. I have many reasons as to why we cannot and should not support such a recommendation.
Those words are attributed directly to the Member speaking on behalf of the Conservative Party, a former Minister. He was speaking to a motion put down by this Party in opposition to the testing of the Cruise missile. He went on to say:
However, I will limit myself in this short and gratis time to saying that we agreed to the modernization of nuclear weapons in 1979.
He was speaking about the Conservatives. I want this to be listened to. Again I quote:
The present Government has concurred in the decision which was taken.
Any person with any degree of intelligence reading that could come to no other conclusion but that the Conservative Party was in agreement with the attitude and policy direction of the Government of the day, the Liberal Party. It bears out exactly what we have been saying for the better part of the last three years, that there is no difference. On major issues, there is no difference between the attitude and policy direction that would be taken by the Conservatives over and against the attitude and policy direction that has been taken by the Liberals.
For the Leader of the Opposition to rise with such indignation and attempt to leave the impression that the Conservative Party was opposed to Cruise testing and that my colleague's very well taken statements were somehow or other not an appropriate reflection of what was said by the spokesman of the Conservative Party in 1980 is very difficult for those of us in the House of Commons to absorb. I held him in higher esteem than that. I find it very difficult to imagine what possessed him to rise and make such an obviously inaccurate statement.
Passing on from that, there is an element of concern that must be expresed about the general attitude that prevails within the House of Commons. There is a misunderstanding on the part of many people of the role of the House of Commons. Because the misunderstanding has been held for a long time, the role of the House has deteriorated. People believe that because one Party gains a majority, it therefore has carte blanche to do whatever it believes, to bring forward at any time whatever measures it believes are appropriate, and that the balance of the House of Commons, the Opposition in particular, are being obstructionist if they in one way or another try to stop the Government from passing what the

Opposition may consider to be illegitimate. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, do not adhere to that view of Parliament. I suspect there are others who do not adhere to it.
The Government has the right to bring forward whatever legislative proposals it deems advisable in its so-called wisdom. However, the Opposition also have certain rights and obligations. It is the right of the Opposition, in as constructive a way as possible within the rules, to attempt to stop the Government from passing that which it believes is inadvisable. It has the obligation to do all in its power to keep the Government from putting in place laws that it believes will be of long or shortterm harm to the country as a whole.
Much of the aggravation that has developed in the House of Commons of late has centred around the role of the Opposition and the way the Opposition approaches its tasks and obligations. The most recent example is the ongoing debate over the Government proposal to change the Crowsnest Pass freight rates. I do not intend to deal with the substance of that because that would not be in order. However, I want to make reference to the way in which that and on other occasions other legislation has been brought forward.
The Government will take one of two principles that may find favour as a question of principle with the House of Commons and do as it did in this instance by including two matters of genuine concern across the country. For example, there is the revitalization of the railroads and the disposition of the dominion coal lands, both of which as a matter of principle the majority in the House of Commons would agree ought to be dealt with. How they should be disposed of would become clear as the question was put before the House.
The Government in this instance, however, as it has in other instances, has taken an absolutely unacceptable measure and lumped it in with the other two, making it extremely difficult for Members who are attempting to do their job diligently and well to vote with a clear conscience on the principle of the Government's measure. The Government's measure in fact contains three principles, two of which may well be acceptable and one of which is totally unacceptable.
That is an abuse of Parliament and it is the kind of abuse that worries me. That is the kind of abuse which causes legislation that is unacceptable and which may have a long-lasting, detrimental effect, to go through the House of Commons and become law. It happens because the Government wants to sneak through something which is very contentious and potentially harmful along with measures that are somewhat less contentious and, if properly handled, would be beneficial.
There is no one in this House who disagrees with any proposal to upgrade the transportation system in this country. No one would disagree that as a matter of principle that ought to be pursued. No one in the House of Commons is prepared to deny that it is time we dealt with the dominion coal lands to determine how they should be utilized and who should have jurisdiction over them. To bring forward each of these measures in separate pieces of legislation-they are not tied
together and are not dependent one upon the other-would make good sense, and that is what the Government ought to do.
No one denies the Government's right to propose changes to the Crowsnest Pass freight rate, but that action is not a matter that need be dealt with in conjunction with the upgrading of the transportation system or the disposition of the dominion coal lands. It can and ought to stand on its own, as a matter of principle.
While the position of this Party would be diametrically opposed to the position likely to be taken by the Government and the Official Opposition on the question of the Crow rate, it recognizes that it is the right of the Government to make whatever proposal it deems necessary for its own purpose. It is the obligation of Opposition to do what it can to make sure the things it does not agree with or believes will have a long-term, detrimental effect, are stopped.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, dealing with that one aspect of the way the House of Commons operates, that there is an abuse of Parliament. It is not the kind of abuse about which the Leader of the Opposition was speaking, but in my opinion it is a serious abuse. It is an abuse which stems from the Government wanting to get certain things done and attempting to push them through with other matters that, if at all related, are only marginally related. The Government must look seriously at its tendency to put into what is now commonly called an omnibus Bill-although it may not adequately apply to this-a number of things that are at odds or are not related. Members of Parliament have the right to have matters of principle put before Parliament in a clear, concise way, a way that is not obscured or fogged, a way that enables them to deal with questions singly and vote upon them as their conscience and knowledge dictate.
You know, Mr. Speaker, as I do, that the whole subject of complicated questions has been before Parliament since the beginning of Parliament. The Government of the day-and I suspect this is not an attribute solely applicable to this Government but to many other Governments that have done likewise-may choose to ignore the important principle that questions can be resolved by the House of Commons singly, as a matter of conscience and as a matter of principle. The Government ought to rethink its position on this principle.
There is another abuse which flows from the way the business of the House is being conducted of late. That is the question of asking the Opposition to pass legislation that it has not seen in a single day. I wish that we did not have to do that. It is difficult to accept that Members of the Opposition, without actually having seen the legislation, should be asked in advance of its even being brought forward to give a commitment to deal with it with one day's debate. I do not see that as a useful addition to the way in which Parliament operates and I urge the Government to recognize that it creates problems rather than solves them.
I appreciate that there is a need, on matters of a somewhat less controversial nature, to look at ways in which the Government may proceed with its business in an orderly manner. I do
June 6, 1983

not think the Government should draw the conclusion from that that every single matter it brings forward can be finalized within a time period that it sets down and which is acceptable to it alone.
There are other questions that begin to draw from the value of the House of Commons. A practice has grown up of late that Ministers of the Crown do not make statements in the House. How often have we read in Saturday's newspaper or watched on Friday night television or listened to a radio newscast and realized that a Minister has sneaked across to the Press Gallery at 4.30 on Friday evening to issue a statement of importance without the Opposition being given an opportunity to respond to it and without its being put on record for public consumption at a time when it would be possible to put our positions on the subject forward simultaneously. There are certain Ministers who do this on a regular basis. They tiptoe across, without a word to anybody, and fill the ears of the press full of rhetoric. By seven o'clock on Friday night when the journalists have a chance to see what the Minister has to say, they have to try to track down a Member of the Opposition to get a response to a statement that the Opposition had not heard or has had no opportunity to study. What is the point of making statements by Ministers available to Cabinet, which of course gives the Opposition an opportunity to rebut or enter into some small debate, if that practice is to be misused by not being used at all? That is an area where there has been serious abuse of Parliament.
That is not the practice in Westminster, Mr. Speaker. 1 recall being at Westminster representing this House of Commons at the time of the Falklands crisis. A statement was never made outside the House with regard to that very crucial issue of the time. There was always an announcement that the Minister would be going to the House of Commons to make a statement within moments, and that the Opposition would be able to question the Minister. That is the way public business should be conducted. That is the way debate should be conducted. It must take place inside the House of Commons where the public can view it through television, can hear about it through other media, and can see the responses from the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party to a clear and concise statement made publicly by Ministers in the proper forum. It is an abuse when the Government does not follow that practice.
Then there is the question of Government expenditures. The Government decides it is going to go ahead with a change to the Crow rate but instead of coming to Parliament and proposing it there first, it advertises the program all across the country at public expense, without having had approval and with no indication that it might become law. It spent tens of thousands of dollars of public money on a program that, when it finally came before Parliament, was substantially different from the program it proposed in the first instance and which it attempted to sell to the people of western Canada. That is an abuse of Parliament. There should be no advertising by Government of its programs until after those programs have been brought into the House of Commons and dealt with.
Supply
That, in my judgment, is the sort of thing we should be dealing with. The questions put are questions of fundamental rights. No one denies that the Cabinet, being the Government, has the right to bring forward whatever proposals it deems necessary for the future of this country. However, equally no one can deny that it is not only the right but the obligation of Parliament to deal with those questions in the House of Commons and to dispose of those questions in the way in which Parliament as a whole feels is appropriate and necessary. The adage that it is Government's right to propose and Parliament's right to dispose must be held to be of vital importance.
It is time that this Government, like all Governments, began to understand that to gain a majority at the polls does not give any Party the right to do whatever it pleases, notwithstanding the parliamentary process which is in place. Just to have a majority at the polls does not give a select few individuals, chosen by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), any proprietary rights over the democratic system established to safeguard the people of Canada from a dictatorship which could be set up. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, in looking at this motion, that I feel there is a place for this kind of debate. It is an important motion and it is important for the reasons I suggest. I believe it is a vitally important motion because I believe that in fact Parliament has become somewhat less important, and I regret that that has been allowed to occur.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with part of what the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) says, that this is a debating forum. What concerns me, however, is that we have a Bill dealing with the Crow rate and we cannot get it on to hear both sides of the issue. The New Democratic Party has already made up its mind that the Crow shall go or that the Crow shall stay. Having made up their minds to do this, Hon. Members of that Party have read into the record a series of petitions and things of that nature. We have heard their side. We have heard their opposition. However, I hardly think that that is debate. I would agree with the Hon. Member; let us bring the legislation on, let us debate it, and let the people of Canada see if the Government also has a position to make, rather than hearing just total opposition to it. Is there a case to be made for the Crow Bill or even some amendments to be made to it as it stands at the present time? Your Party would not even let it be introduced, which is not the traditional way to do things around here. Under normal circumstances-and I have been here 15 years-I can think of about two or three occasions when people have refused to allow a Bill even to be introduced. I believe that is an inappropriate use of a parliamentary situation. We are hearing your side, but I do not feel we have had an opportunity to hear what the majority's side has to say about the subject.

I am happy, Mr. Speaker, that you brought that to the Hon. Member's attention. He tends to abuse the rules regularly. What the Hon. Member is saying, Mr. Speaker, is not factual, although it is true that, having had prior knowledge of the content of the Bill, this Party said that it did not believe that the Bill should come before Parliament. I contend that that is an appropriate use of the rules. Given that the Minister spent tens of thousands of dollars advertising his proposals, telling everyone in the land what was contained in them, I feel that once we knew what was in them, and once we recognized the immeasurable harm it would do, we had an obligation to begin by saying that we did not think the Bill should be introduced. Beyond that, however, there has been considerable time for debate.
I put to the Hon. Member honestly that there are three distinctly different principles in the Bill. No one can convince me that we cannot deal with the disposition of the dominion coal lands separate and apart from the upgrading of the railroads or the disposition of the Crowsnest Pass freight rate agreement. No one can convince me that we cannot deal with the upgrading of the railroads separate and apart from the disposition of the dominion coal lands or from the disposition of the Crowsnest Pass freight rate agreement. Nor can anyone tell me that to deal with the Crowsnest Pass agreement requires us to deal simultaneously with the upgrading of the transportation system or the disposition of the dominion coal lands.
What we are saying is that those are three distinctly differently principles. If the Government would like to go ahead with two of them right now, before the end of June, then we would be quite prepared to facilitate that. However, the Crowsnest Pass freight rate is a question of serious contention across this country, a question of great complication, which cannot be dealt with in a short period of time. We feel, given the number of speakers, given the nature of the Government's intention to impose time allocation, that we must stop it now until it agrees to at least divide the three principles. That seems to me to be the way Government ought to operate.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to hear the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain giving his views on the Crow rate agreement, and that is my point. That is the kind of debate we should have. Perhaps it should be divided into three parts, I really do not know.
Let it go to committee.
Hear, hear!

The Hon. Member is clapping. I said perhaps that is the way it should be, but who will know? Who in Canada will know? If I had not asked the Hon. Member the question through you, Mr. Speaker, the country would not have known that that Party would like it divided into three parts. We have an opportunity to debate it here. Let us debate it. Let us make the decision about whether or not in committee it should be split. It is obvious that that Party has made up its mind. It is a minority Party. It has the right to stall, to block
and to do as much as it can. However, there comes a time when we should have debate. That is what Parliament is all about. I do not believe that the Government is receiving its just due here in having its opportunity to debate a Bill which it is satisfied is for the general benefit, not only of the people of western Canada, but the people in all of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to say that I honestly believe there is not a single Member in this House who does not have a sincere desire to improve Parliament and to make this institution one that is eminently deserving of respect, because whenever extreme actions or tactics are used by any Members of the House to undermine the parliamentary process and Parliament's credibility, I think everyone of us has to pay for this in some way, and I feel it is very bad for a country where individual and collective freedoms are as respected as they are. I want to make it clear, first of all, that within the framework of the debate on this motion, we on this side of the House are willing to listen to any constructive proposals for improving the parliamentary process and making Parliament more effective, more modern and better able to meet the needs of Canadians.
However, when we read the text of the motion itself, it is clear that it lacks substance and that it is rather partisan. It would have been easy, this morning, to use the text of the motion, especially after the speech by the Acting Leader of the Official Opposition, to make this debate a purely partisan and political one, pointing out various abuses and making this a confrontation which, in the final instance, would have proved to be sterile and would not have enhanced the prestige of this institution, and would certainly not have increased the stature of our politicians in this country.
However, I would prefer to take this opportunity to express some views on our attempts, in recent years, and especially during this session, to improve the parliamentary process, and also to point out certain specific facts which speak for themselves and will illustrate the point I wish to make, and finally, I would like to set the record straight on some statements that have been made.
I would like to start by correcting the record and I hope it will be clear once and for all. The Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has been here for over a quarter of a century and should know what happened in 1960 because he was here and most of us were not. I hear a good friend like the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who just left the chamber, supporting the affirmation made by the Leader of the Opposition when he said that the Business of Supply was forced down the throat of the Opposition through closure in
June 6, 1983

the year 1960. That is misleading the House and is unacceptable. I cannot understand how Members who were here at the time can so lightly support an affirmation such as this which has been made more than once during the last three years. It is absolutely contrary to the reality, the truth and to what happened in fact.
During the speech of the Leader of the Opposition I asked that I be provided with the proper extracts from the records of the House of Commons. I see the Hon. Member for St. John's East has come back and I hope he will convey the message to his dear leader, the Hon. Member for Yukon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Beloved leader.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
His beloved leader, I am sorry. The reference is clear and it appears on page 4230 of Hansard for December 20, 1968, when the fourth and fifth reports of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization of the House were presented and adopted by all Parties unanimously. The questions were put and agreed to. As shown in the Journals of the House of Commons at page 554, December 20, 1968, we see the corroboration of the fact that the new Standing Orders, including 25 Opposition days and the whole Business of Supply we are now applying, were not carried on division, not forced through by closure. The questions were put to the House and they were agreed to unanimously.
So I hope that once and for all the Leader of the Opposition will stop saying the Business of Supply has been imposed on the Opposition. It was a decision taken by Parliamentarians, just like the decision we took a few months ago to experiment in parliamentary reform. That was supported unanimously by Members on both sides of the House. I hope that in future the Hon. Member for Yukon, who has been here for over a quarter of a century, would stop misleading the House on this in order to try and score cheap political points when the facts are absolutely contrary to what he is saying.

Mr. Speaker, when I started my speech, I said that I would also like to put certain facts on the record. For a better understanding of what I am about to say, the public must realize that in a week in Parliament-before the present experiment, that is, last year and in previous years-only four days were available to the Government to consider subjects, bills and measures introduced by the Government. On average, the Opposition was usually given one day on which it would select the subject for debate. If we consider the time that has been spent on a number of important measures in the national interest during this session, we realize how limited the Government is in its flexibility and its ability to introduce for debate enough measures in the national interest to meet the needs of a society as diversified as ours.
Perhaps I may refer Hon. Members to the major debates we have had during this session, of which we are particularly proud. The Leader of the Opposition alluded to the fact that this has been the longest session in history, having gone on for
Supply
more than three years. We are nevertheless proud of that fact, because this session has produced many exceptionally important measures that have made history and that are vital to the entire country. I am referring to what we have done in very basic and specific areas such as the Constitution, energy and the economy. As soon as we started this session, we made it quite clear that we intended to be agressive, to table major issues and introduce appropriate measures, even if they might be controversial, because we felt it was necessary for the country, that it was our responsibility as a Government, and also because we knew these measures would come before Parliament, which would have an opportunity to debate them, we hoped, in a constructive and civilized manner. Unfortunately, that has not always been the case, and I shall talk about this later on. In any case, most people are aware of what happened on certain occasions.
Take the Constitution, for instance. In his motion, the Leader of the Opposition blames the Government, and I quote:
-for its continuing attempts to reduce Parliament and Parliamentary government to an irrelevant appendix in the formulation and application of major national policy decisions-
I should think the term national policy applies particularly well to patriation of the Constitution, the Charter of Rights, the inclusion of the principles sharing, equity and equalization in the constitutional resolution, as well as a new amending formula that was adopted.
However, in order to consider this national question, we had to use ... I am not complaining, but it is a fact we should not overlook and which explains why so often other measures had to wait their turn, and why some sessions, during which a great deal of business is considered, will tend to last longer. The debate on the Constitution, not counting the meetings of the Committee, took up 38 days of debate in the House on the various motions we introduced, both before and after the debate in committee. If we add the months of televised debate on this important subject in committee, we will realize that Parliament, which consists not only of the House of Commons and the Senate but also of their respective committees, was asked to debate a very important issue, that Parliament was therefore involved in these decisions and that in the final instance, the constitutional resolution we brought before Parliament is a resolution that was debated in the House of Commons, before the Special Joint Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate, and, finally, in the Senate. The Constitution we have now is a constitution made in Canada, but considering the issue we are debating this morning, it is entirely proper to say that it is a constitution that was made in Parliament.
To think there are people who claim that we have downgraded Parliament. I wonder how they could forget the time the House spent not so long ago on issues that are of vital importance to the entire country. Thirty-eight days is quite a long time, when we realize that the Government has four days a week, which means that in one month, there are 16 days

June 6, 1983
Supply
available, on average, for considering government business. This means that for more than two and a half months, aside from the days set aside for the Opposition, there was no time for anything else on the floor of the House except the debate on the Constitution. Almost one third of the time of the House of Commons was used for the exclusive consideration of constitutional resolutions, not including the debate in committee.
Another major issue was the National Energy Program. This major debate took 112 days of Government time in the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps we should realize that 112 days represents nealy a full year of the time of the House, spent exclusively on energy and the Bill on our national energy policy-112 days, which means 377 hours and 22 minutes, and this in addition to the six days of debate on the Budget, which was also debated in the same period, six days that are not included in the 112 days, and neither am I including 15 or 16 days when the division bells rang in Parliament, when the Progressive Conservatives, in a manner that is totally unacceptable, systematically paralyzed the Parliament of Canada and prevented any debate from taking place.
When I said that 112 days of Government time were used to debate the energy issue during this session, that does not include the 15 or 16 days we heard the division bells, and this means that for all practical purposes, we have once more had almost nine months or a full parliamentary year devoted almost exclusively to energy.
Another vital issue has been the economy. Parliament has considered the subject on many occasions. If I am not mistaken, we have had four budgets, in addition to statements on the economy, and I may remind the House that in the previous budget, we proposed our 6 and 5 policy to fight inflation, which has proved to be a tremendous success. I think it is irresponsible and unrealistic of an Opposition Member to claim that this major anti-inflation policy was put into effect outside Parliament. The policy was debated here in the House of Commons. It was analyzed, amended and debated in the Parliament of Canada, which was asked to consider one of the most pressing issues of the moment, in the middle of a recession: how do we prepare for economic recovery and how do we fight against inflation? This was followed by the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), which included $4.8 billion to stimulate the economy and create jobs in this country. People who say that the major economic issues were not debated in Parliament are either half or totally asleep, or they are entirely ignorant of what is going on in Parliament or they are not being sincere, but I hardly think that is the case.
Mr. Speaker, the fact is that as far as the 6 and 5 policy is concerned, we must not forget the time the House of Commons
needed to debate this policy so that we could obtain the results we have today, at this very moment, namely, that inflation is now down to 6.6 per cent, from 13 per cent in August 1981. The bank rate, the rate set by the Bank of Canada, is now 9.5 per cent. We all remember that only a year and a half ago, mortgage rates were over 20 per cent. Our 6 and 5 policy has worked, it has benefited the entire country and has produced concrete results. We realize this now. How was this brought about? By the Government, who originated the plan, but also as a result of debate in Parliament. The Parliament of Canada was asked to consider this important question, and in fact did so for a grand total of 72 days, the equivalent of two full semesters of our parliamentary year, or 236 hours and five minutes, when it debated Bill C-131, Bill C-132, Bill C-133, Bill C-139 and Bill C-125, which are directly connected with our 6 and 5 policy and to amendments to update the Income Tax and remove any uncertainty in the business world.
Therefore, if we look at three major issues-the economy, energy and the Constitution-we realize that in the Parliament of Canada, in the House of Commons and in committee, a considerable number of days and hours were spent on debate on these issues, time that could therefore not be used to consider other issues of perhaps lesser importance nationally but nevertheless vital to certain activity sectors in this country. That is why, since we have been considerate and have shown respect for this institution, and since we have allowed debate on major issues despite the Opposition's often provocative attitude, we are asking Opposition Members for their cooperation regarding debate on less controversial measures. Now what happened then? Even before we could implement the parliamentary reform which we managed to get approved by the House because of a committee that worked in good faith and the cooperation of the House as a whole, and in spite of the unacceptable objections of a few senior members of the Progressive Conservative Party, we were able to carry out the present experiment, Mr. Speaker.
However, even before we proposed this parliamentary reform to the House, I had suggested to the Progressive Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party that we have a rational debate on a number of bills. I refer to last fall, to October 1982, when I submitted a list of 16 bills to the two House Leaders of the Opposition, and more particularly to the present Leader of the Progressive Party, the Acting Leader, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). There were 16 bills about which I said: "Listen, the session has been going on for two years, a reform is forthcoming, a committee is working on it; let us show that we want Parliament to work, let us forget the silliness of the bell-ringing incident that you, the Progressive Conservative Party, brought about, let us forget your filibuster during the constitutional debate, and let us try to show the people that parliamentarians on both sides of the
June 6, 1983

House can agree so that Parliament may work in an efficient, civilized, modern and productive manner."
The Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party never agreed to negotiate any aspect of a single of those 16 bills, neither to draw up our work schedule and to determine the length of the debate nor to decide how much time the various stages of those bills required, quite the opposite! Undoubtedly that was not in keeping with the strategy of the Progressive Conservative Party which had to come to grips with its internal leadership problems and which opted instead for making every attempt to catch the Government off guard in a vote so as to trigger an election before having to decide the fate of their leader in Winnipeg and at the Civic Centre in a few days.
It is unfortunate that the Official Opposition chose to undermine the parliamentary process as a result of its internal squabbles. It is a sad comment, Mr. Speaker, but I think that was the real cause of the shameful incidents we have witnessed. Members of the Progressive Conservative Party have been frustrated, first in December 1979 when they lost power after only 37 days into the session, and ever since in their internal leadership crisis which has dictated their approach, their outlook and their behaviour with respect to the parliamentary system. For the first time in our history, we saw a party resort to such drastic means as the bell ringing incident to prevent rather than promote debate, to undermine the very essence of Parliament, in short, to torpedo Canada's democratic system by putting an end to any constructive debate in the House and systematically preventing this institution from tackling major issues.
I conclude by expressing the hope that after my remarks Hon. Members will keep in mind the fact that we have shown respect for Parliament and that we want to do even better, but that calls for co-operation from both sides of the House and not only from the Government. That cannot be achieved without good will on the part of the Opposition, and we are always prepared to do our best so that Parliament will be ever more efficient, humane, modern and respected by the people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question. One wonders, when one hears the Government House Leader, with all of the confidence he has about the many things we are doing wrong, why he does not simply call an election and take the issue to the polls, to the people.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That's exactly the problem.

Why does he not do that right now? I would invite him to do it right now. Mr. Speaker, the Government House Leader has continually referred to what he feels was unanimous support for the rules passed in 1969. I want to draw the Government House Leader's attention to the book by John B. Stewart entitled "The Canadian House of Commons, Procedure and Reform", specifically to page 250. The Government House Leader has continually suggested that these rules

were passed unanimously. On page 250, Mr. Stewart makes the following point:
Six months later, on 20 June 1969, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization fulfilled the order of the House by recommending three new standing orders: 75A, 75B, and 75C. These were adopted, without alteration, by the House at the sitting of 24 July 1969, but only after closure had been used to terminate a filibuster by all the opposition parties.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Standing Orders 75A, B and c? You're not talking about the same thing. That is not supply.

I would refer to Hansard for July 24, 1969, at page 11619, wherein it is reported there was a vote in which the yeas and nays were recorded. The Government, the majority, steamrollered through the closure and then on July 24, 1969, the rules were finally passed, on closure, on a recorded vote in which the Opposition of the day voted against the rules.
I want to ask one simple question of the Government House Leader. Should we change Hansard and the book by John B. Stewart, or should the Government House Leader revise his version of what happened when those rules came in, in order to comply with the truth?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You're all mixed up, Doug.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just one point. One simply has to read and understand. The Hon. Member is talking about a vote after closure that took place merely to implement Standing Order 75a, b and c. That is absolutely not what I was talking about and that is absolutely not what his interim leader was talking about in his speech. We were talking about Opposition days, the Business of Supply. That is the reform and those are the rules to which I was referring and to which his leader was referring when I quoted Hansard and the Journals.
I would seek unanimous consent to table the proper extract from Commons Debates and the House of Commons Journals that very clearly demonstrate that in fact the Business of Supply, the Opposition days, were adopted unanimously by this House of Commons. I hope this consent will not be denied.
